title: Workers' Compensation and Injury Duration: Evidence from a Natural Experiment
research_question: Does an increase in the level of weekly cash benefits paid to injured workers lengthen the duration of time they spend out of work recovering from workplace injuries? The aim is to quantify how the generosity of injury-related income replacement affects how long claimants remain off the job.
data_description: The study draws on administrative workers' compensation claim records from two U.S. states, Kentucky and Michigan. Each observation is an individual injury claim, with information on the date of injury, the date of return to work (used to construct injury duration in weeks), the weekly benefit amount received, pre-injury wages, demographic characteristics of the claimant (such as age, gender, and marital status), industry, and the nature and body part of the injury. Claims span periods around state-level changes in the maximum weekly benefit, allowing comparison of injury spells before and after these changes. The samples include temporary total disability claims, with injury duration as the principal outcome and weekly benefit generosity as the key explanatory variable.
institutional_context: Workers' compensation programs in the United States are administered at the state level and provide cash benefits to workers injured on the job, typically replacing roughly two-thirds of pre-injury wages subject to a statutory maximum weekly benefit. Because of this cap, increases in the maximum primarily raise benefits for higher-wage workers while leaving benefits unchanged for lower-wage workers whose replacement amounts already fall below the cap. Kentucky and Michigan each enacted substantial increases in their maximum weekly benefit, generating sharp, legislatively determined changes in the generosity of compensation for one group of injured workers but not another at essentially the same point in time. This policy setting creates a natural comparison between affected and unaffected claimants spanning the benefit changes.
